title: Using binocular rivalry to assess cultural differences in spatial-frequency processing of faces.
abstract: Cultural experience shapes attention, memory, and some aspects of visual processing, but it remains unclear whether it influences perceptual selection when incompatible images compete for awareness. We preregistered a binocular rivalry study to test whether Eastern and Western observers differ in the relative weighting of low- versus high-spatial-frequency information during initial perceptual competition. Forty-nine Western participants (U.S.-born, ≤ 2 years abroad) and 43 Eastern participants (recent East Asian arrivals, ≤ 5 years in the U.S.) viewed dichoptic pairs of spatially filtered faces (Albert Einstein, Marilyn Monroe). Image size was varied across five levels to shift retinal spatial frequency content, allowing estimation of each observer's "balance point"-the size at which low-pass and high-pass filtered faces were equally dominant. In a second component of the study, a filtered image of one face was pitted against an unfiltered image of the other face to assess the competitive strength of isolated spatial-frequency bands against broadband-image rivals. Increasing retinal image size enhanced the dominance of high-pass information. However, mean balance points did not differ between cultural groups, and no reliable association emerged with measures of participants' levels of acculturation or cultural values. The results suggest that the initial outcome of perceptual competition in binocular rivalry is largely independent of cultural background and that the mechanisms governing this competition operate similarly across observers from different cultural backgrounds. OPEN PRACTICES STATEMENT: The study was preregistered online ( https://osf.io/pgyqv ). Final analyses deviated from the plan in that we used the quickpsy Package in R (instead of fitting a 2nd-degree polynomial using MATLAB's curve fitting toolbox) to generate a cumulative normal curve which better characterized the relationship between image sizes and task performance. This also allowed us to use t tests rather than ANOVAs. In addition, sample sizes exceeded the original plan to allow for exclusions and for exploratory individual difference analyses. After reviewing the stereopsis test measure-but without comparing data from the two groups-the team decided that getting six of the nine circles correct (instead of the preregistered criterion requiring nine out of nine circles) would be sufficient to demonstrate stereopsis. We did not use response times as an exclusion criterion for individual trials, and our additional exploratory analyses focused on the self-report measures of culture rather than those included in the preregistration. We deemed these exploratory analyses to be more of interest, given the focus of the paper, than those originally planned or the sample characteristics did not support further follow-up analyses (e.g., uneven distributions of urban/rural background and gender). Data and code are available at https://osf.io/st473 and https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/ST473 .

title: Safety and quality of life outcome of trans-anal irrigation for chronic constipation in Parkinson's disease: a pilot study.
journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
abstract: Constipation in Parkinson's Disease (PD) is the main and most disabling non-motor symptom. Laxatives, prebiotics and probiotics are therapeutic options for neurological bowel diseases, and recently, Trans-Anal Irrigation (TAI) has also been considered in poor responders to medical treatment. The primary aim was to evaluate safety and indication of TAI in treating PD constipation. A pilot, prospective, observational, cohort study enrolled PD patients with chronic constipation. At baseline, TAI was proposed. Patients who accepted TAI had a neurological and proctological assessment at baseline (T0), 6-month (T1) and 12-month (T2). Twelve patients accepted TAI. At T1 and T2, no side effects were recorded. TAI patients showed statistically improved proctological assessment (p < 0.001) and unchanged neurological scores except for the PDQ-39 questionnaire (p < 0.001) at T2. TAI is safe for constipation treatment in PD. Improving intestinal transit might ameliorate quality of life, laying the foundation for new therapeutic strategies.

title: Neuroprotective effects of the petroleum ether fraction of Teucrium polium in free and lipid nanoparticle formulations on cognitive deficits and oxidative stress in an ICV-STZ-induced Alzheimer's-like rat model.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline, oxidative stress, and neuronal loss. Current pharmacological treatments provide only partial symptomatic relief. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of the petroleum ether fraction of Teucrium polium (T. polium), administered in both free and lipid nanoparticle formulations (T. polium-LNP), in a rat model of AD-like pathology induced by intracerebroventricular streptozotocin (ICV-STZ). Adult male Wistar rats were divided into five groups: Control, ICV-STZ, ICV-STZ + Memantine, ICV-STZ + T. polium, and ICV-STZ + T. polium-LNP. Cognitive function was assessed using the Morris water maze (MWM) and novel object recognition (NOR) tests. Serum oxidative stress markers-including malondialdehyde (MDA), total antioxidant capacity (TAC), and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity-were measured. Hippocampal CA1 histopathology and hippocampal mRNA expression of Bax, Bcl-2, and p53 were also evaluated. The ICV-STZ-induced AD-like model was associated with memory impairment, increased serum MDA levels, reduced TAC levels and SOD activity, and hippocampal CA1 neuronal damage, accompanied by increased Bax and p53 expression and decreased Bcl-2 expression. Treatment with T. polium and T. polium-LNP improved cognitive performance, particularly spatial memory in the MWM, and attenuated several pathological changes. Both treatments reduced serum MDA levels and decreased CA1 neuronal degeneration. In this experimental AD-like rat model, both formulations of T. polium were associated with improvements in cognitive performance, serum oxidative status markers, and hippocampal tissue changes. Although T. polium-LNP showed numerically greater effects on several outcomes, direct comparisons between the free T. polium extract and T. polium-LNP were statistically significant only for CA1 neuronal damage. Further mechanistic and long-term studies are needed to clarify the potential relevance of these findings to AD-related neuroprotection.

title: Integrated QTL mapping and CRISPR screening in pooled iPSC-derived microglia reveals genetic drivers of neurodegenerative risk.
abstract: Mounting evidence implicates microglia in neurodegeneration, but linking disease-associated genetic variants to target genes and cellular phenotypes is hindered by the inaccessibility of these cells. We differentiated 261 human induced pluripotent stem cell lines into microglia-like (iMGL) cells in pools with phenotypic (differentiation, phagocytosis and migration) and single-cell transcriptomic readouts. Burden analysis of deleterious variants detected 36 genes influencing microglial phenotypes. Expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) analysis identified 7,121 eQTL-associated genes and 79 colocalizations across four neurodegenerative disease genome-wide association studies, half of which had limited prior evidence of causality. Integration of eQTL and phenotypic associations highlighted the role of disease-relevant variants, including LRRK2 and TREM2 acting through microglial phagocytosis. A coupled CRISPR screen identified a role for TREM2 in phagocytosis and highlighted the importance of cell type in the directionality of phenotypic effects. By contextualizing variant effects within iMGLs in different inflammatory states, we provide a comprehensive framework for interpreting the function of risk loci in neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Author Correction: Trans-ancestry genome-wide analyses of bipolar disorder in East Asian and European populations improve genetic discovery.
Microglia mediate motor memory decay through activity-dependent phagocytosis of myelin sheaths.
abstract: Experience-dependent changes in myelination are important for motor learning, with newly generated oligodendrocytes contributing to the formation of new myelin. However, motor memories decay over time and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored. Here we show that motor memory decay is linked to changes in memory-associated myelin sheaths resulting from microglial phagocytosis in mouse brain. Mechanistically, reduced activity of motor memory engram cells lowers oligodendrocyte expression of the 'don't eat me' signal from Cluster of differentiation 47 (CD47), facilitating microglial phagocytosis and driving myelin loss. Knockout of CD47 from motor memory-associated oligodendrocytes increased microglial phagocytosis of myelin sheaths and accelerated the decay of motor memory, whereas overexpression of CD47 showed opposite results. Moreover, microglia phagocytose myelin sheaths and synapses independently. Our findings reveal that microglial phagocytosis of motor memory-associated myelin sheaths leads to the decay of motor memory. Since various types of memory require myelination in the brain, this mechanism may contribute to the decay of other memory types.

title: Fetal hemoglobin fraction: a potential predictor of late-onset sepsis in very preterm infants.
abstract: Late onset sepsis (LOS) is included between the so-called oxidative stress-related diseases in preterm infants. Increasing evidence supports a protective role of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) against oxidative stress. We hypothesized that HbF blood fractions measured during the first weeks of life may be associated with the risk of developing LOS. We carried out a retrospective observational study on 166 preterm infants with gestational age <30 weeks. The primary endpoint of our study was the comparison of HbF fraction values between infants who developed LOS and those who did not during the first week of life. Fifty-six (34%) infants had LOS at the mean age of 14±8 and 22±15 days of life. Infants with LOS had lower HbF fractions from the 14th day of life (HbF14) to 36 weeks of postmenstrual age. Regression analysis showed that higher HbF14 decreased (OR 0.974, 95% CI 0.956-0.992; P=0.004) the risk of LOS. In ROC analysis, HbF14 showed moderate discriminative ability in predicting LOS, with an AUC of 0.676 and 95% CI 0.593-0.758. Lower HbF fractions during the first weeks of life were associated with an increased risk of LOS, with HbF14 emerging as an independent protective factor. These findings confirm the role of HbF in modulating susceptibility to oxidative stress-related complications in this vulnerable population and the importance of maintaining its levels high. • Low fetal hemoglobin (HbF) fractions are associated with increased risk of oxidative stress-related complications of prematurity. Late-onset sepsis (LOS) is included among oxidative stress-related diseases. • Infants with LOS had lower HbF fractions from the 14th day of life to 36 weeks of postmenstrual age. Regression analysis showed that higher HbF fraction at 14 days of life is associated with decreased risk of LOS.

title: Mitochondria-lysosome crosstalk in health and disease.
abstract: Mitochondria and lysosomes are central regulators of cellular metabolism, nutrient sensing, cellular quality control, and stress adaptation. Although traditionally studied as independent organelles, it is now evident that they operate as an integrated functional network through multiple modes of communication, including membrane contact sites, signaling pathways, and selective vesicular trafficking. Disruption of this crosstalk is increasingly recognized as a common feature of mitochondrial disorders, lysosomal storage diseases, neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and aging, highlighting its importance for cellular and tissue homeostasis. While mitophagy has long been considered the principal interface between mitochondria and lysosomes, recent discoveries have revealed a much broader communication landscape in which bidirectional signaling, ion exchange, lipid transfer, and mitochondria-derived vesicles coordinate organelle function independently of bulk degradation. In this Review, we discuss the molecular mechanisms that mediate mitochondria-lysosome communication, emphasizing emerging concepts in inter-organelle signaling and membrane contact biology. We further examine how disruption of these pathways contributes to human disease and consider the growing evidence that restoring mitochondria-lysosome communication, rather than targeting either organelle in isolation, represents a promising therapeutic strategy.

title: The world's most precious brain samples - and what they teach us about being human.
Should we move from artificial intelligence to artificial life?
Polygenic liability to loneliness increases psychosis risk through adolescent loneliness: evidence from the EU-GEI study.
abstract: Social isolation and loneliness are associated with schizophrenia, yet their distinct genetic contributions and developmental pathways across the psychosis spectrum remain poorly understood. Using data from the EU-GEI study (2045 patients and 2456 healthy controls), we examined whether genetic liability to loneliness and social isolation increases psychosis risk through a two-step strategy: first testing whether polygenic scores (PGS) for loneliness and four isolation-related traits (derived from UK Biobank GWAS) were associated with first-episode psychosis (FEP), schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (SSD), symptom dimensions, and retrospectively reported loneliness and social isolation during childhood and adolescence; and second testing whether these developmental experiences mediated the relationship between genetic liability and psychosis. Genetic liability to loneliness (LNL-PGS) was associated with increased psychosis risk in the combined sample and specifically with FEP, independent of schizophrenia and depression genetic risk, with stronger effects in males. In contrast, a PGS indexing frequency of family and friends' visits (VISITS-PGS), as a proxy for objective isolation, was associated with SSD diagnosis-particularly in females-and greater negative symptom severity. At the developmental level, LNL-PGS predicted prolonged loneliness during adolescence (ages 12-16) among patients, especially males, while VISITS-PGS only predicted lower sociability in childhood in healthy controls. Mediation analyses revealed that adolescent loneliness partially mediated the association between LNL-PGS and psychosis risk, accounting for 21% of the total effect and up to 27% in males. Together, these findings support partially distinct genetic and developmental mechanisms-with sex-specific contributions-linking perceived loneliness and objective social isolation to psychosis risk, and highlighting adolescent loneliness as a potential target for early preventive interventions.

title: A multimodal consensus parcellation of the human brainstem and its applications in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: The brainstem is a highly conserved integrative hub that is essential for arousal, emotion, and motor control, which are functions profoundly affected in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, low signal-to-noise ratios in neuroimaging of subcortical nuclei hinder the construction of brainstem parcellations that integrate complementary functional and structural information, limiting our understanding of circuit-specific pathology. Here, we developed the Multimodal Consensus Brainstem Parcellation (MCBP), a fine-grained atlas that integrates high-resolution naturalistic 7 T functional MRI and diffusion MRI acquired in the Human Connectome Project (N = 160). The MCBP exhibits high reproducibility, symmetry, and homogeneity. Using this parcellation, we find a pronounced structure-function dissociation within the brainstem. Furthermore, MCBP reveals a hierarchical brainstem organization aligned with the unimodal-to-transmodal axis, distinguishing motor execution from visually guided motor preparation that closely resembles the Somato-Cognitive Action Network (SCAN). Crucially, in an independent PD cohort, MCBP-derived connectivity improved disease classification and symptom-severity prediction compared with existing brainstem atlases, supporting its sensitivity to both categorical disease status and dimensional clinical variation. Feature decoding revealed a dual-system pattern of PD-related alterations across sensorimotor and cognitive-affective networks. Notably, it identified a specific brainstem-limbic circuit linked to emotional heterogeneity, providing circuit-level insights for distinguishing anxiety- and depression-related neuropsychiatric PD subtypes independent of motor severity. Beyond distinguishing and grading disease, the MCBP-derived connectivity measure also outperformed those derived from existing atlases in predicting multidimensional behavioral traits in a large healthy participant cohort (N = 976). Together, MCBP offers a fine-grained, biologically grounded brainstem parcellation and a framework for probing circuit-specific changes in neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Unveiling the functional specialisation of human white matter circuits with naturalistic stimuli.
abstract: Functional MRI (fMRI) has traditionally focused on grey matter activations, overlooking the contribution of white matter pathways to brain organisation. Yet evidence suggests that white matter constrains, modulates, and integrates signals across distant regions. Here, we introduce a framework to map the functional specialisation of white matter circuits using fMRI scans collected while participants watched naturalistic videos. By leveraging ecologically valid stimuli, this method captures cognition as it naturally unfolds. Integrating fMRI with brain connections, we derived a functionally grounded parcellation of the connectome, challenging conventional cortical-based cognitive taxonomy. Distinct cognitive profiles emerged for association and commissural fibres, with association pathways preferentially linked to language-related processes and commissural pathways to executive and motor functions, affirming the functionally heterogeneous nature of white matter systems. An artificial intelligence framework applied to independent datasets confirmed the robustness and functional relevance of the identified parcels. This open-access framework also enables the interactive exploration of white matter functional organisation, offering a new lens on the neural bases of cognition.

title: Longitudinal resting-state EEG-based modeling predicts phenoconversion and delineates heterogeneity in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder.
abstract: Isolated REM sleep behavior disorder is a high-risk prodromal syndrome for Lewy body diseases but highly heterogeneous. Neurophysiologic markers resolving this heterogeneity and predicting phenoconversion remain limited. We applied Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn) modeling to longitudinal resting-state EEG from a prospective cohort of 285 participants. SuStaIn identified a progressive degenerative subtype (Subtype 2), characterized by delta/theta increases and lower MoCA scores, and a posterior beta-low subtype (Subtype 1), which was longitudinally unstable and of uncertain independent prognostic significance. Longitudinal validation demonstrated substantial subtype shifting in Subtype 1 and stage advancement predominantly in Subtype 2. In Kaplan-Meier analysis, subtype shifting and accelerated annual stage advancement (ΔStage≥2) identified individuals at exceptionally high phenoconversion risk with survival approaching 0-15% by 7.5 years. These findings extend SuStaIn beyond cross-sectional inference by incorporating longitudinal subtype-shifting and stage-advancement features to stratify prodromal heterogeneity and predict neurodegenerative progression.

title: Unveiling the impact of goal types: enhancing self-efficacy in rehabilitation robotics.
abstract: In response to the growing need for effective and engaging stroke rehabilitation, this study examined how different goal-setting strategies influence self-efficacy and task performance during upper-limb motor learning with a soft pneumatic exoskeleton robot. One hundred participants practiced boccia while wearing the robot and were assigned to process (skill-focused), outcome (score-focused), shift (process-to-outcome), transform (feedback-based adjustment), or control conditions. Bayesian multivariate regression showed that self-efficacy was higher in the outcome (b = 21.13, 95% CrI [7.94, 34.24]), shift (b = 18.19, 95% CrI [4.84, 31.06]), and transform (b = 21.22, 95% CrI [8.59, 34.21]) conditions relative to the process condition. Structural equation modeling further indicated that perceived robot softness was positively associated with general task self-efficacy and negatively associated with negative perceptions of the robot. These findings extend our understanding of how human-robot interaction contributes to self-efficacy and highlight the importance of aligning goal-setting strategies with robot design in rehabilitation contexts.

title: Ultrasensitive detection of alpha-synuclein oligomers in human plasma using optimized nano-QuIC.
abstract: Early diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) is critical, as clinical symptoms typically emerge only after substantial neuronal loss. While α-synuclein (α-Syn) oligomers in blood are promising biomarkers for early detection, their clinical utility is limited by their low abundance and the presence of inhibitory components in the plasma matrix. To address these limitations, we tailored the Nanoparticle-enhanced Quaking-Induced Conversion (Nano-QuIC) platform specifically for the ultrasensitive detection of α-Syn oligomers in human plasma. We identified critical reaction determinants by investigating buffer pH, ionic strength, detergent types, and shaking conditions. Furthermore, the integration of silica nanoparticles (siNPs) proved essential in mitigating plasma matrix interference, ensuring robust and reproducible protein aggregation. Under these optimized conditions, the assay achieved a detection limit of 100 pg/mL for α-Syn oligomers spiked into human plasma. These results demonstrate that our adapted Nano-QuIC platform provides a highly sensitive and minimally invasive method for detecting pathological α-Syn species, offering a significant advancement toward the development of early-stage PD diagnostics.

title: A genetic platform to deconvolve efficacy and toxicity reveals the on-target effects of CDK11 inhibition in vivo.
abstract: The cyclin-dependent kinase CDK11 is an understudied kinase that has been the subject of conflicting reports regarding its function in cancer. Here, we combine genetic and pharmacological approaches to demonstrate that CDK11 is a critical regulator of cancer cell survival that is required for RNA splicing and the expression of homologous recombination genes. Inhibition of CDK11 disrupts genome stability, promotes the retention of intronic sequences in mature mRNAs, and induces synthetic lethality with PARP inhibitors. Through integrative analysis of functional genomics datasets, we identify heterozygous deletions of chromosome 1p36 - which encompasses CDK11 and its activating cyclin CCNL2 - as a recurrent and predictive biomarker of sensitivity to CDK11 inhibition. To assess the therapeutic potential of CDK11, we establish a genetically-engineered mouse model that allows us to differentiate between the on-target and off-target effects of CDK11 inhibitors in vivo. Using this platform, we demonstrate that MEL-495R, an orally bioavailable CDK11 inhibitor, induces widespread on-target toxicity, revealing a narrow therapeutic index. Experiments with a chemically distinct CDK11 inhibitor similarly reveal minimal anti-cancer activity at tolerable doses. Together, these findings define CDK11 as a core cancer dependency, uncover a chromosomal deletion that sensitizes tumors to CDK11 inhibition, demonstrate that on-target toxicity limits the efficacy of CDK11-targeting therapies, and provide a generalizable strategy for deconvolving drug efficacy and toxicity in vivo for novel oncology targets.

title: Familial risk, shared familial risk and partner-associated risk of neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases.
abstract: Brain diseases cluster within families, but the extent of familial risk across different brain diseases remains unclear. In this study, 10,620 participants reported 7 neurodegenerative and 9 psychiatric diseases in 53,361 family members. Familial risk was assessed by determining if a first-degree relative affected by a brain disease increased the risk of the proband having the same disease. Shared familial risk referred to increased risk of the proband having a different brain disease. Similarly, we assessed (shared) partner-associated risk using partner data. Familial risk was present across all neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases studied. Shared familial risk was present between some neurodegenerative diseases, while prominent between all psychiatric diseases. Four associations were identified between neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases. (Shared) partner-associated risk was almost exclusively seen in psychiatric diseases. Overall, neurodegenerative diseases exhibited distinct familial patterns, while psychiatric diseases shared a continuum of familial and partner-associated susceptibility.

title: Three-photon population imaging of subcortical brain regions.
abstract: Monitoring large-scale neuronal activity in deep brain circuits is crucial for understanding the principles of brain function. However, existing large-scale cellular-resolution imaging techniques are limited in imaging depth and cannot monitor activity in areas deeper than the cortex in the intact brain. To address this challenge, we developed a Large Imaging Field of view Three-photon (LIFT) microscope with a FOV of > 3 mm2. LIFT combines high-numerical-aperture optimized sampling, using a custom scanning module, with deep learning-based denoising, to enable population imaging in subcortical brain regions of mice and deep cortical regions of rats. We demonstrate calcium imaging in the intact mouse brain from more than 1500 cells across CA1, the surrounding white matter, and adjacent deep layers of the cortex, and show population imaging with high SNR at a depth of 1.2 mm in the rat cortex. The LIFT microscope offers versatility in imaging scale and rate and was built entirely from off-the-shelf components.

title: Dietary interventions and stroke clinical outcomes: a systematic review.
journal: International journal of stroke : official journal of the International Stroke Society
abstract: Optimal nutrition is biologically essential for supporting neural repair mechanisms post-stroke, yet clinical guidelines provide limited and non-specific dietary recommendations that are largely extrapolated from primary cardiovascular prevention rather than stroke recovery populations. To systematically review and synthesise evidence from randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effects of food-based or whole-diet interventions on clinical outcomes in adults with stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA), including disability, neurological function, cognition, mood, quality of life, and stroke recurrence. Following Cochrane and PRISMA guidelines, four databases (Medline, Embase, CINAHL, CENTRAL) were searched to February 2026 for RCTs testing oral dietary interventions (≥4 weeks) in adult stroke/TIA survivors. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2. Eight RCTs (n=15,974) were included (1 low risk, 6 some concerns, 1 high risk). Quantitative meta-analysis was precluded by marked heterogeneity. Interventions included salt substitution (n=2), Mediterranean diets (n=2), ketogenic diet (n=1), partial meal replacement (n=1), Trigona honey (n=1), and soy milk (n=1). Reduced-sodium salt substitution decreased stroke recurrence (RR 0.86, 95%CI 0.77-0.95) and mortality (RR 0.88, 95%CI 0.82-0.96) in large Phase III trials, while Mediterranean diets improved quality of life (EQ-5D mean difference: 10.1, 95%CI 1.8-18.4). For functional recovery, small Phase I/II pilot trials yielded exploratory, domain-specific proof-of-concept signals (e.g., post-exercise soymilk enhancing walking performance; Trigona honey improving MoCA scores), but were constrained by high susceptibility to Type I errors and effect size overestimation. Ketogenic diet improved NIHSS (5±2 vs 7±2, p<0.01) and disability (mRS: 2±1 vs 3±1, p<0.05), but was accompanied by high adverse event rates (keto-flu 25%, GI distress 15%, hyperlipidemia 10%). Salt substitution and Mediterranean diets show clear promise for secondary prevention and recovery. Given the limited and heterogeneous evidence base, high-quality, phase-specific RCTs are urgently needed to establish stroke-specific nutrition strategies.

title: Health-related quality of life in patients with solid cancer treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors: the ARON-MOUSEION-18 systematic review and meta-analysis.
journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
abstract: Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) contributes to the value of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), but assessment and reporting remain heterogeneous. This PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261330878). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for RCTs of adults with solid tumors comparing ICI-based regimens with non-ICI controls and reporting global HRQoL with the EORTC QLQ-C30 GHS/QoL scale or EQ-5D-3L/5L visual analogue scale (VAS). Pooling required a visit-specific adjusted between-group estimate with a 95% confidence interval (CI) or standard error. Random-effects models (restricted maximum likelihood, Hartung-Knapp adjustment) were used. Clinical relevance was assessed using instrument-specific MID benchmarks. Eighty-two RCTs were included: 42 in the quantitative and 40 in the narrative synthesis, 40 reported EORTC QLQ-C30 GHS/QoL, 10 EQ-5D-3L VAS, and 14 EQ-5D-5L VAS. All pooled trials evaluated anti-PD-1-based regimens. The pooled LSMD for EORTC QLQ-C30 GHS/QoL was 1.78 points (95% CI 0.71-2.86; p = 0.002; I2 =71.9%). Neither EQ-5D VAS differ significantly. Most trial-level estimates were below the MID, and no trial showed clinically meaningful deterioration. Favorable estimates were concentrated in open-label active-control, advanced/metastatic and lung cancer trials. Anti-PD-1-based therapy results in no clinically important difference in global HRQoL compared with non-ICI controls: the small average advantage is below the MID and concentrated in open-label active-control trials. Interpretation is shaped by trial design, comparator, setting, assessment timing, and incomplete PRO reporting. Standardized PRO reporting is needed across cancer settings and ICI classes.

title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation targeting bilateral primary motor cortex: Promotion of corticospinal remodeling and motor recovery after incomplete spinal cord injury.
abstract: Functional recovery after incomplete spinal cord injury remains limited largely because injured corticospinal pathways have insufficient capacity for structural remodeling and reconnection. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation targeting the primary motor cortex (M1) can modulate cortical excitability, but whether it drives corticospinal tract remodeling after spinal cord injury and how neurotrophic mechanisms contribute to this process remain poorly understood. Glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor-related signaling may provide a biological link between cortical stimulation and regenerative responses within the injured nervous system. A multilevel translational design integrating transcriptomic analysis, animal experiments and exploratory clinical evaluation was applied. Public spinal cord injury transcriptomic datasets were integrated to identify shared repair-associated genes and pathways. Bilateral M1-targeted repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation was administered in a T10 incomplete spinal cord injury rat model, with or without systemic anti-glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor antibody treatment. Behavioral, electrophysiological, histological and molecular analyses were performed to evaluate functional recovery, corticospinal tract remodeling and glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor-related signaling. Finally, an exploratory randomized controlled trial was conducted to assess functional, electrophysiological and serum biomarker responses to repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in patients with incomplete spinal cord injury. Integrated transcriptomic analysis identified 51 shared differentially expressed genes linked to neurotrophic regulation, neural remodeling and PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling. In rats with incomplete spinal cord injury, bilateral M1-targeted repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation improved locomotor recovery and corticospinal function, promoted corticospinal tract remodeling, and modulated a glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor-associated PTEN/PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling profile, whereas anti-glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor antibody treatment partially attenuated these repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation-associated effects. Spinal RNA sequencing further revealed enrichment of pathways related to axonal growth and synaptic function. Clinically, real repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation was associated with superior functional and electrophysiological outcomes and higher serum levels of neuroplasticity-associated biomarkers than sham stimulation. In summary, bilateral M1-targeted repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation was associated with corticospinal tract remodeling and functional recovery after incomplete spinal cord injury. Preclinical findings support a contributory role of glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor-associated PTEN/PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling in repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation-induced neural repair, whereas the exploratory clinical results provide preliminary translational evidence without demonstrating the same molecular mechanism in humans.

title: Extracellular vesicle-mediated neuroimmune remodeling across synucleinopathies: Therapeutic implications of cell-type specificity and central-peripheral crosstalk.
abstract: Synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy, are characterized by convergent α-synuclein misfolding, impaired proteostasis, and chronic neuroinflammation. Despite these shared pathological features, these disorders exhibit distinct inclusion-bearing cell profiles, vulnerable neural circuits, immune phenotypes, and clinical progression rates, with neuronal inclusions dominating in Parkinson's disease/dementia with Lewy bodies and oligodendrocyte pathology predominating in multiple system atrophy. Extracellular vesicles have emerged as critical modulators integrating these multifaceted pathogenic processes. Secreted by neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, extracellular vesicles cross biological boundaries to deliver diverse bioactive molecules and mediate intercellular communication. This review synthesizes current evidence to propose that extracellular vesicles serve as context-dependent mediators connecting intracellular proteostatic stress to local glial reactivity and systemic immune regulation. Extracellular vesicle-associated α-synuclein maintains a seeding-competent conformation, enters recipient cells, and triggers templated aggregation and inflammatory signaling, although its exact pathogenic contribution relative to free α-synuclein and non-vesicular transmission routes remains undefined. Extracellular vesicle cargo dynamically reshapes microglial and astrocytic activation, oligodendroglial homeostasis, neuronal survival, blood-brain barrier integrity, and peripheral immune recruitment. Extracellular vesicles exert bidirectional effects: pathological extracellular vesicles amplify neurotoxicity, while homeostatic or engineered extracellular vesicles restore proteostasis, optimize immune homeostasis, and facilitate neural tissue repair. Advanced techniques including immunocapture, real-time quaking-induced conversion, and single-vesicle profiling enhance the sensitivity and resolution of extracellular vesicle-based biomarkers, enabling improved discrimination among synucleinopathy subtypes. However, clinical translation is hampered by extracellular vesicle heterogeneity, inaccurate cell-origin tracing, pre-analytical variability, insufficient standardization, and limited causal in vivo and longitudinal evidence. It is concluded that extracellular vesicles function as integral components of a dynamic, multilayered communication network, with their outcomes determined by cellular origin, cargo, recipient type, disease stage, and anatomical context. Standardized protocols, longitudinal cohorts, and mechanistic models are indispensable for developing reliable extracellular vesicle biomarkers and safe extracellular vesicle-targeted therapies for synucleinopathies.

title: Frequency-dependent entorhinal cortex stimulation differentially modulates spatial working memory and CA1 network dynamics.
abstract: Entorhinal cortex deep brain stimulation is a promising approach for modulating memory circuits; however, how stimulation frequencies across different frequency bands shape task-relevant hippocampal dynamics and working memory remains unclear. In this study, C57BL/6J mice were implanted with entorhinal cortex stimulation and CA1 recording electrodes and trained in a delayed T-maze spatial working memory task. Entorhinal cortex deep brain stimulation was delivered at 15, 50, or 130 Hz using an intermittent 30-minute protocol before behavioral testing, with a sham-control group. CA1 local field potentials and spiking activity were recorded during the T-maze task. We analyzed oscillatory power, theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, and spike-local field potential phase-locking in putative pyramidal neurons and interneurons. Post-mortem immunohistochemistry was used to quantify the excitatory synaptic marker vesicular glutamate transporter 1 expression and the inhibitory marker glutamate decarboxylase 67. Baseline performance was balanced across groups. Within-subject comparisons showed that 15 Hz entorhinal cortex deep brain stimulation significantly improved choice accuracy without altering decision latency. This behavioral improvement was accompanied by increased CA1 theta-, low-gamma-, and high- gamma-band power, enhanced firing and theta-phase locking in putative interneurons, and increased postmortem vesicular glutamate transporter 1 expression density. In contrast, 50 Hz stimulation did not improve choice accuracy and produced divergent cell-type-specific changes in phase-locking, including enhanced theta-locking in putative interneurons but reduced theta-locking in putative pyramidal neurons. Although 130 Hz stimulation increased theta-high- gamma phase-amplitude coupling and GAD67 expression, it did not significantly improve choice accuracy. Sham-operated animals showed no significant behavioral improvement across repeated testing sessions. The frequency of entorhinal cortex deep brain stimulation determined distinct behavioral, electrophysiological, and histological profiles during delayed spatial working memory. The 15-Hz protocol produced the only coherent profile, characterized by improved memory performance accompanied by enhanced CA1 theta/gamma oscillations, increased interneuron theta-phase locking and excitatory synaptic marker density than those observed with the 50- or 130-Hz protocols. These findings indicate that stimulation frequency is a critical determinant of entorhinal cortex-targeted memory modulation.

title: Topological visual perception and innate defense: Shared subcortical pathway for early diagnosis and neural plasticity intervention in brain disorders.
abstract: The superior colliculus-pulvinar-amygdala subcortical pathway has long been recognized as a key pathway mediating innate defensive behaviors and rapid threat detection. Emerging evidence indicates that this pathway additionally supports unconscious topological visual perception, a primitive, evolutionarily conserved visual function that extracts global object structure independently of emotional valence. Notably, topological perception and threat detection are functionally distinct yet engage shared anatomical nodes within the superior colliculus-pulvinar-amygdala pathway, likely through partially segregated local subcircuits. As an emotion-neutral, robust, and unconscious marker, topological perception is hypothesized to be a potential functional probe for early subclinical dysfunction across brain disorders. Cumulative cross-sectional evidence suggests that functional impairments within the superior colliculus-pulvinar-amygdala pathway may emerge at early or subclinical stages across multiple neurodegenerative, mood-related, and neurodevelopmental disorders (e.g., Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, affective disorders, schizophrenia, and autism spectrum disorder), though longitudinal cohort data are still required to verify whether these alterations constitute genuine preclinical pathological events that precede overt clinical symptoms. Importantly, this pathway retains strong intrinsic neural plasticity and regenerative potential, supporting its suitability for early non-invasive intervention. This review summarizes the dual functions of the superior colliculus-pulvinar-amygdala pathway in fundamental topological visual perception and threat-detection-related defense, and outlines its specific structural and functional abnormalities across various brain disorders. We further systematically evaluate interventions including behavioral training, real-time neurofeedback, temporal interference stimulation, transcranial ultrasound, and pro-regenerative pharmacologic agents to restore circuit function and enhance neural plasticity. We propose that the superior colliculus-pulvinar-amygdala pathway represents a promising novel transdiagnostic target for early diagnosis and neural plasticity-based regenerative intervention in brain disorders, although validation in large-scale human longitudinal cohorts is still required.

title: The Clinimetric Spectrum of Poor Response After Treatment for Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy.
abstract: Clinicians regularly modify treatment in chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) because of insufficient response, yet it is unclear how changes over time in the recommended outcome measures inform these decisions. We therefore explored which changes were observed in patients deemed to have an insufficient treatment response. We selected patients with CIDP who were previously included in various prospective studies, in whom first-line treatment was changed within 6 months due to deterioration or insufficient improvement. Changes in two disability and two impairment measures were analyzed according to commonly used minimal clinically important difference (MCID) thresholds. We included 16 patients. Median time to treatment change was 12 weeks (IQR 6 to 19). In seven patients (44%), treatment change coincided with deterioration on all available outcome measures, and this occurred within 12 weeks of treatment in 6 patients. Earlier change was associated with more severe baseline disability and impairment, and greater magnitude of deterioration. In seven patients (44%), treatment was changed despite (limited) improvement on one or two outcome measures; all of these observations occurred after 12 weeks. Earlier treatment change seemed to be associated with clear deterioration on most outcome measures, while later treatment changes were mainly associated with insufficient improvement, reflected by a combination of improvement and worsening in different clinical outcome measures. Our findings suggest that poor response to treatment requires a nuanced consideration of multiple outcome measures, taking the magnitude and consistency of change into account in relation to treatment duration.

title: Developmental and age-acquired somatic mutations in neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Classical genetic studies have assumed a uniform genome across the body, but humans are genetic mosaics harboring distinct somatic mutations acquired during development and aging. The role of somatic mosaicism in neurodegenerative disease remains poorly understood. In this article, we review somatic mosaicism in two contexts: developmental mosaics arising during embryogenesis and age-associated clonal expansions. Developmental mosaics are established contributors to neurodevelopmental disorders, with emerging evidence linking them to adult-onset neurodegeneration, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and Alzheimer's disease. Postnatal clonal expansions in microglia and hematopoietic cells may further promote systemic inflammation and disease progression. We synthesize these findings into a framework in which developmental and age-acquired mutations contribute to neuronal vulnerability, disease heterogeneity, and the pathogenesis of sporadic neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Beyond memory strengthening: noradrenergic control of memory specificity.
abstract: Emotionally significant events are typically remembered better and for longer than mundane experiences. This emotional memory enhancement critically depends on arousal-induced norepinephrine release within the brain. Beyond memory strengthening, recent work shows that noradrenergic activity also shapes the specificity, detailedness, and temporal precision of memories during both early consolidation and systems consolidation. In this review, we synthesize recent findings from human and animal research spanning molecular, circuit, systems, and behavioral mechanisms to propose an integrative framework for how emotional arousal-induced noradrenergic activity affects neural systems that regulate memory specificity and systems consolidation dynamics. The proposed framework refines current models of memory under emotional arousal and may have relevant implications for stress-related psychopathologies.

title: Special issue of autonomic neuroscience: Basic and clinical on the concept of visceral Interoception in health and disease.
Epidemiology and Modifiable Risk Factors for Benign Prostatic Enlargement and Related Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis.
abstract: Benign prostatic enlargement (BPE) and related lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS/BPE) represent highly prevalent health issues globally, and related modifiable risk factors are recognized as a sensitive topic for prevention strategies. We summarized evidence on associations between the epidemiology of these conditions and modifiable risk factors. We performed a systematic review with meta-analysis of studies in MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols. Twenty-four studies (four cohort and 20 cross-sectional) were included. Pooled synthesis showed positive associations between waist circumference (WC) >90 cm (two studies) and body mass index >24 kg/m2 (three studies) and prevalent BPE in Asian males. WC >90 cm was positively associated with prevalent moderate-to-severe LUTS in the same ethnicity (two studies). Narrative synthesis showed associations between abnormal adiposity and prevalent BPE/moderate-to-severe LUTS also in non-Asian males as well as associations between the epidemiology of LUTS and physical activity, alcohol intake, metabolic syndrome, and smoking status in both ethnicities. Associations between dietary/sleep patterns and LUTS epidemiology were evident in Asian males. The certainty of evidence was very low. BPE and related LUTS represent highly prevalent health issues with global incidence and prevalence rates projected to increase in the next decade. Positive associations between high adiposity indices and prevalent BPE have been observed in both Asian and non-Asian males. Modifiable risk factors associated with moderate-to-severe LUTS include: abnormal adiposity indices, levels of physical activity, smoking status, alcohol intake, metabolic syndrome (all in both ethnicities), and sleep/dietary patterns (in Asian males). However, definitive clinical recommendations could not be provided.

title: A cadaveric investigation of the posterior tibial tendon transfer: Which route provides the shortest distance to the lateral cuneiform?
journal: Foot and ankle surgery : official journal of the European Society of Foot and Ankle Surgeons
abstract: Posterior tibial tendon (PTT) transfer is commonly performed for foot drop. Limited tendon length may compromise fixation, and effect of transfer route on available tendon length is unclear. This cadaveric study compared three transfer routes to determine which preserved the greatest tendon length. Ten cadaveric specimens underwent PTT transfer. Each specimen underwent three transfer routes, tested over and under the extensor retinaculum. A 15-kg load simulated tendon anchoring and tendon distance in tunnel (TDIT) was measured using a digital caliper. Repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc comparisons was performed. Over-retinacular routing preserved more TDIT than sub-retinacular placement (mean difference = 3.66 mm, p = .008). The interosseous route lateral to the anterior compartment produced the greatest TDIT, exceeding the circumtibial route (p = .027). The interosseous route lateral to the anterior compartment, routed over the extensor retinaculum, produced the greatest TDIT and may optimize fixation when tendon length is limited. 5.

title: [Research progress on the mechanism of role of 5-hydroxytryptamine in sepsis-associated intestinal injury].
journal: Zhonghua wei zhong bing ji jiu yi xue
abstract: Sepsis-associated intestinal injury (SAII) is a clinical syndrome that develops during sepsis progression, characterized by impaired intestinal motility, digestion and absorption, barrier damage, microbiota dysbiosis, and dysregulated immune-inflammatory responses. As a common complication of sepsis, SAII represents a major contributor to multiple organ dysfunction and death. Given that SAII development involves complex processes including inflammation, oxidative stress, gut barrier dysfunction, and microbiota dysbiosis, no specific and effective treatment is currently available in clinical practice. Therefore, elucidating the pathophysiological mechanisms of SAII and identifying potential therapeutic targets are essential for improving septic patients' outcomes. 5-Hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) is a key monoamine neurotransmitter and paracrine/autocrine signaling molecule, widely distributed in both peripheral tissues (e.g., the gut) and the central nervous system. In the gut, 5-HT functions as a key neurotransmitter and regulatory molecule, critically involved in intestinal motility, secretion, sensory signaling, and mucosal immunity. Existing studies demonstrate that during sepsis, intestinal 5-HT levels are dysregulated, and its various receptor subtypes show aberrant activation or suppression. Through multiple mechanisms, including modulation of inflammatory responses, immune cell activity, intestinal barrier function, gut microbiota, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis, these alterations drive and exacerbate intestinal injury. Therefore, 5-HT and its receptor subtypes represent promising therapeutic targets for SAII prevention and treatment. Modulating 5-HT synthesis or metabolism, or selectively targeting specific receptor subtypes, may offer novel therapeutic strategies for SAII. This article systematically synthesizes existing research to review the potential mechanisms of 5-HT and its receptors in SAII, with the aim of providing a theoretical basis and novel insights into SAII pathogenesis and targeted therapeutic development.

title: Intervening contexts reshape hippocampal-cortical retrieval states and later source attribution.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Memories are often reactivated in one context and only later judged with respect to where they originally occurred. We tested how an intervening retrieval context shapes neural representations and later source memory. In two fMRI tasks, participants (both male and female) encoded objects within contextual backgrounds, completed an immediate retrieval test in which object cues appeared against either the original background or a different background, and subsequently judged each object's original context on a neutral screen. Shifted cueing contexts reduced source accuracy and biased errors toward the intervening context, despite no detectable difference in immediate recognition or associative-memory performance. Representational similarity analyses showed that encoding patterns reflected original-context structure, whereas immediate-cue-period patterns were broadly organized by the cued (i.e., currently visible) context. On shifted trials, activity patterns showed greater similarity to encoding-derived templates for the cued context than for the original context. Across participants, greater differentiation of original-context similarity between consistent and shifted cueing in posterior hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex was associated with better source memory after a contextual shift. Within participants, precuneus contextual engagement and dorsal anterior cingulate context alignment predicted later source choices, with similar relationships after adjustment for immediate recognition responses. Later source attribution therefore depended on the contextual state expressed when an item was re-encountered, not simply on reinstatement of the original event.Significance statement Remembering is often described as bringing up the past, but memories are frequently reactivated in new contexts before we judge where they came from. We show that this intervening context can bias later source attribution even when that context is no longer visible at final test. Using two fMRI tasks, representational similarity analysis and trial-level source-choice models, we found that cue-period activity was organized by the context present during cueing and that specific context-state signals predicted later memory choices, whereas item reinstatement did not. Source-memory errors can therefore reflect contextual information encountered after the original event, not only failures to recover the original context.

title: Phase-Structured Neuronal Recruitment in Motor Cortex during Skilled Movement Reorganized Early after Stroke.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Skilled forelimb movement engages both oscillatory and spiking activity in the motor cortex. However, how oscillatory phase organizes neuronal recruitment during behavior remains unclear. Here, we performed longitudinal bilateral recordings of local field potentials and single-unit activity in the rat (male) caudal forelimb area during a single-pellet retrieval task before and after stroke. Stroke altered spectral organization and redistributed neuronal recruitment across hemispheres. In the CFA contralateral to the reaching forelimb, which was the lesioned hemisphere, firing rates decreased and spike timing became more variable, whereas spike-LFP phase consistency increased in low-frequency bands. In contrast, the CFA ipsilateral to the reaching forelimb showed increased firing and reduced low-frequency phase consistency. These results demonstrate that early post-stroke motor cortical reorganization does not simply weaken neural activity but reshapes neuronal recruitment into a phase-structured form within ongoing oscillatory activity, providing insight into the dynamical principles underlying motor cortical reorganization during skilled movement.Significance Statement Skilled movement depends on coordinated interactions between populationlevel oscillations and neuronal spiking, but how this organization changes after cortical injury remains unclear. Using longitudinal bilateral recordings during skilled forelimb behavior, we show that early post-stroke reorganization is not characterized by a uniform loss of cortical activity. In the CFA contralateral to the reaching forelimb, firing was reduced and spike timing became more variable, yet low-frequency spike-LFP phase consistency increased. The ipsilateral CFA showed the opposite pattern, with increased firing and reduced low-frequency phase consistency. These findings demonstrate that firing output and spike-phase organization can reorganize independently after stroke, revealing a phase-structured dimension of motor cortical activity that is not captured by firing rate alone.

title: Multidimensional dynamics of object representations in the human visual system.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Natural image representations are distributed across many dimensions of visual cortex activity, but little is known about how the multidimensional structure of these representations evolves over time following stimulus onset. Herewe examined the temporal dynamics and latent dimensional structure of natural object representations in large-scale EEG and MEG data from male and female human participants. We also compared these datawith leading representational models derived from large-scale human similarity judgments and deep neural networks. Our findings reveal a rapid expansion of stimulus dimensionality in the brain, which peaks within 100 milliseconds and gradually decays over hundreds of milliseconds. The dynamics of these dimensionality changes tracked the decoding accuracy for both behavioral embeddings and neural network features, suggesting that dimensionality may be a general indicator of representational expressivity. Interestingly, the dimensionality of the neural representations could not be fully explained by a leading behavior-based model or deep neural network. Follow-up experiments showed that the remaining neural variance carried additional perceptually relevant information not yet explained by leading models. Together, these findings reveal previously unrecognized complexity in measurements of dynamic human brain responses to natural objects.Significance Statement When we look at an object, our brains rapidly construct a rich internal representation of what we see. Using large-scale, time-resolved brain recordings from people viewing thousands of natural images, we find that the brain rapidly expands its representational complexity within the first 100 milliseconds, sustaining this richness for hundreds of milliseconds thereafter. A leading behavioral model and a large-scale deep neural network do not fully account for this complexity - yet the unexplained brain activity is not noise: people can reliably use these residual neural patterns to judge image similarity. These findings challenge the assumption that such brain recordings are informationally limited and reveal structure in the human visual system that future models will need to explain.

title: Hemichorea following treatment for oligodendroglioma.
The Intersection of Synaptic Plasticity and Engram: Dual Foundations Shaping the Destiny of Episodic Memories.
abstract: The engram has been proposed as the physical substrate of specific memories. Over the past decade, research has elucidated the neural mechanisms governing how a sparse population of neurons is recruited into an engram and how they functionally mature to sustain memory storage. Specifically, the intrinsic excitability of neurons at the moment of memory encoding biases the incorporation of neurons into an engram. While this selection occurs immediately after learning, these neurons initially remain "silent" and are incapable of driving memory recall through natural cues. Evidence suggests that de novo protein synthesis-dependent synaptic potentiation between engram neurons is required for these engrams to become functional. In this article, we review the neural mechanisms underlying engram allocation and the synaptic mechanisms underlying the functional maturation of engram neurons across different brain regions. Furthermore, we provide an overview of the synaptic remodeling that supports the system-wide reorganization of engram networks during the establishment of remote memory (systems memory consolidation). We also examine how the engram is flexibly updated upon memory extinction and retrieval from the perspective of synaptic plasticity. Finally, we highlight novel methodologies and tools for visualizing and manipulating synaptic architecture, discussing how these advancements will refine our understanding of the interplay between engrams and synaptic plasticity.

title: Sleep and Neurodegenerative Diseases: Understanding the Bidirectional Relationship.
abstract: Sleep and circadian rhythm disturbances are pervasive across the spectrum of Lewy body disorders (LBDs), including Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. Accumulating clinical, epidemiologic, and neurobiological evidence supports a bidirectional relationship between sleep dysfunction and neurodegeneration, in which pathologic processes disrupt sleep-wake regulation, and impaired sleep may exacerbate neurodegenerative mechanisms, including impaired proteostasis, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and failure of glymphatic clearance. In this review article, the authors synthesize evidence linking sleep and circadian disturbances with LBDs across prodromal, early, and advanced disease stages.

title: Persistent Hypersomnia in Neurological Disease: Mechanisms, Diagnosis, and Management.
abstract: Hypersomnia in neurological disease is characterized by excessive sleep quantity in a day, distinct from excessive daytime sleepiness. It arises from the disruption of brainstem-hypothalamic-thalamic arousal circuits and neurotransmitter systems. Hypersomnia significantly impacts quality of life, safety, cognition, rehabilitation, and caregiver burden across conditions, including Parkinson's disease, stroke, traumatic brain injury, and multiple sclerosis. Systematic evaluation with polysomnography/multiple sleep latency testing distinguishes hypersomnia from fatigue and apathy. Treatment involves mechanism-guided approaches: addressing reversible causes (medications, sleep disorders), then pharmacotherapy with wake-promoting agents or stimulants, with special considerations for epilepsy, autonomic dysfunction, and neurodegenerative disease.

title: Circadian Rhythm Disruptions: Causes, Consequences, and Treatment Approaches.
abstract: Circadian rhythms are intrinsic biological cycles of approximately 24 h that regulate sleep, metabolism, hormone secretion, cardiovascular function, and other physiologic processes. Coordinated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus and molecular clock genes such as CLOCK, BMAL1, PER, and CRY, these rhythms are influenced by external cues, especially light, meal timing, exercise, and social interactions. Circadian disruption contributes to sleep-wake disorders, metabolic dysfunction, cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, psychiatric illness, and cancer risk. Assessment tools include melatonin measurements, questionnaires, sleep diaries, and actigraphy. Treatment focuses on optimizing zeitgebers, particularly light exposure and melatonin, to restore circadian alignment and improve health outcomes.

title: Sleep and Aging: Understanding Changes and Promoting Healthy Sleep in Older Adults.
abstract: Sleep disturbances and disorders (e.g., sleep-disordered breathing and insomnia) are commonly observed in aging populations and are associated with numerous health conditions (e.g., cardiovascular disease) that can impede everyday functioning and well-being. Thus, this review focuses on conceptual frameworks accounting for various factors related to aging adults' sleep, benefits and challenges of using various sleep assessments across aging populations, and considerations for optimizing treatment efforts to improve their sleep health. With increased longevity and divergent life-course experiences, various diagnostic and treatment strategies will be necessary to develop personalized approaches to sustaining good sleep health.

title: Updates in Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Behavior Disorder.
abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia characterized by dream enactment behaviors resulting from loss of normal REM sleep atonia. Increasingly, RBD is recognized not only as a sleep disorder but as a critical neurologic entity, strongly associated with α-synuclein-related neurodegenerative diseases This review highlights recent advances in the understanding of RBD across its clinical spectrum, diagnosis, pathophysiology, and emerging role as a biomarker of neurodegeneration. Current management focuses on safety and symptomatic control, while ongoing research explores disease-modifying therapies and positions RBD as a key platform for neuroprotective clinical trials.

title: Induction of motor system plasticity using transcranial magnetic stimulation.
abstract: This chapter reviews magnetic brain stimulation techniques designed to induce neural plasticity in the motor cortex. Originally developed as repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation with a fixed rate, several protocols have since emerged to produce longer-lasting effects more efficiently, such as theta-burst stimulation, paired associative stimulation, repetitive paired-pulse TMS, and quadripulse stimulation. Additionally, transcranial static magnetic stimulation applies static magnetic fields to the brain. These techniques have advanced our ability to modulate cortical excitability and promote neuroplasticity, particularly influencing excitatory and inhibitory circuits in the motor cortex in a manner mimicking long-term potentiation and long-term depression. This would help us better understand how cortical circuits can be reprogrammed. Clinically, these methods leverage the brain's adaptability and hold therapeutic potential for neurologic and psychiatric disorders, including stroke rehabilitation, depression, neurodegenerative diseases, and enhancing motor learning and cognitive function. Future research will aim to refine these protocols, reduce inter-individual variability, and explore new clinical applications by incorporating genetic factors for personalized stimulation, which will improve the precision and effectiveness of brain stimulation techniques in treating various disease conditions.

title: Effect of noninvasive brain stimulation on voluntary movements.
abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a noninvasive technique used to probe and modulate brain activity that has significantly enhanced our understanding of voluntary motor control. By disrupting or enhancing neural function with temporally precise ("online") or sustained ("offline") stimulation protocols, TMS has revealed how primary motor, premotor, and posterior parietal cortices contribute to motor execution, reaction time, action selection, reach planning, and grasp kinematics. Single-pulse and repetitive TMS protocols enable precise mapping of both the timing and the functional role of a brain region's involvement in voluntary movement. Dual-coil TMS protocols further allow for the measurement and modulation of trans-cortical connectivity, clarifying how distributed brain areas coordinate complex actions. These various TMS approaches have also helped elucidate mechanisms of motor learning, cortical plasticity, and use-dependent adaptation. TMS is a useful tool for establishing causal links between neural circuits and voluntary motor control and holds therapeutic potential for motor rehabilitation.

title: Clinical applications of brain-computer interfaces in the motor system.
abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable direct interaction between neural activity and external devices or neuromodulatory systems, offering novel approaches for restoring, rehabilitating, and modulating motor function following neurologic injury and disease. Over recent decades, BCIs have progressed from experimental demonstrations of operant conditioning to clinically relevant technologies applied in stroke, spinal cord injury, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, movement disorders, and other motor syndromes. This chapter presents a critical, clinically focused review of motor BCIs, with emphasis on clinical applications rather than technical fundamentals. Key topics include invasive and noninvasive signal acquisition methods, anatomic targets for recording and stimulation, decoding and artificial intelligence approaches, and actuator systems such as robotics, functional electrical stimulation, and spinal or cortical neuromodulation. Particular attention is directed toward hybrid and closed-loop architectures that connect motor intention with sensory or motor outcomes through precise temporal contingency, a fundamental requirement for promoting adaptive neuroplasticity. Evidence from randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, and emerging invasive studies is evaluated, highlighting areas with substantial clinical support, particularly poststroke motor rehabilitation and adaptive deep brain stimulation for Parkinson disease, as well as fields undergoing active translational development. The chapter also addresses efficacy measures, treatment durability, and current barriers to widespread clinical implementation, while outlining future directions involving minimally invasive implants, adaptive decoders, and network-level neuromodulation.

title: Clinical use of transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with electroencephalography in the motor system.
abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) has emerged as a powerful technique to investigate cortical physiology and network dynamics in vivo. By directly recording the cortical response to noninvasive brain stimulation, TMS-EEG enables the assessment of cortical inhibitory and excitatory mechanisms, oscillatory activity, and effective connectivity within large-scale network organization independently of the corticospinal output pathways. These properties make TMS-EEG particularly valuable for studying disorders affecting the motor system. This chapter reviews the principles of TMS-EEG in the motor system and summarizes its application in four major neurologic disorders leading to motor network dysfunction, including stroke, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis. Across these, TMS-EEG has provided novel insights into disease-specific mechanisms, including cortical disinhibition, network reorganization, diaschisis, pathologic oscillatory activity, and alterations in brain complexity. Furthermore, growing evidence suggests that TMS-EEG-derived measures are associated with clinically relevant outcomes such as motor impairment, recovery potential, disease progression, and treatment response. Although methodologic challenges and the need for larger and longitudinal cohorts remain, TMS-EEG represents a promising approach for characterizing network dysfunction and may contribute to future treatment strategies in neurology.

title: Immune Checkpoint Dysregulation in Inflammatory Neuropathies: An Exploratory Study.
abstract: Inflammatory neuropathies (IN), such as Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP), are characterized by peripheral nerve injury driven by immune activation, although the precise mechanisms remain unknown. Dysregulated immune checkpoint molecules (ICMs) are known to trigger autoimmunity and inflammation; however, the role of ICMs is not well elucidated in IN. We investigated the gene expression levels of ICMs, such as programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1) and cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen-4 (CTLA-4), as well as their respective ligands (CD274, and CD86/CD80) in IN. This case-control, cross-sectional, hospital-based study included 67 patients with IN (GBS = 47, CIDP = 20) and equal number of healthy controls. Gene expression levels of PDCD1, CD274, CTLA4, CD86, and CD80 were quantified using ddPCR and correlated with the clinical and electrophysiological parameters. PDCD1, CTLA4, CD274, and CD86 gene expression levels were significantly higher in IN than in healthy controls (p = 0.001, 0.017, 0.001, and 0.006, respectively). In GBS, PDCD1 and CD274 expression levels were significantly increased compared with controls (p = 0.001 and 0.003, respectively), whereas in CIDP, the expression levels of CTLA4, CD274, CD86, and CD80 were higher than in controls (p = 0.050, 0.033, 0.003, and 0.016, respectively). CTLA4, CD86, and CD80 expression levels were greater in CIDP than in GBS (p = 0.049, 0.001, and 0.014, respectively). This study demonstrates differential expression of ICMs in GBS and CIDP. The immune checkpoint pathways may play a crucial role in the pathogenesis of inflammatory neuropathies, which warrants further exploration in larger cohorts.

title: Antimicrobial peptides that cross the blood-brain barrier: systematisation of data on known representatives and prospects for their use in CNS diseases.
abstract: The limited permeability of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is one of the key obstacles in the development of new drugs for treating brain disorders. Most small molecules fail to reach therapeutic concentrations within the brain parenchyma; this causes systemic toxicity, low efficacy, and the development of drug resistance in pathogens and tumor cells. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent a large, heterogeneous group of substances that exhibit a wide range of therapeutic effects and often show low toxicity toward healthy cells. Their ability to cross the BBB independently makes them promising drug candidates for the treatment of infectious, inflammatory, and oncological diseases of the brain. To date, only a small number of peptides are known to combine antimicrobial properties with their ability to cross the BBB. Despite the significant potential of this group of molecules, experimental data on the transport of AMPs across the BBB remain fragmentary and are often obtained using incomparable experimental conditions; moreover, some earlier findings require re-evaluation in light of current knowledge regarding the barrier function of the BBB. This review provides the first systematic compilation of scattered data on peptides that combine antimicrobial activity with the capacity for transcytosis across the BBB. Three key groups of peptides have been identified and analyzed: 1) proline-rich insect AMPs (apidaecin 137, oncocin, and drosocin); 2) endogenous mammalian neuropeptides (substance P, neuropeptide Y, vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP)); 3) cell-penetrating peptides with AMP properties (penetratin, transportan 10, pVEC). The combination of antimicrobial activity and the ability to cross BBB appears to be an achievable and reproducible characteristic for peptides of various origins, thus underlying the clear need for their discovery and development.

title: From Burden to Breakthrough: A Roadmap to Disentangle Fatigue in Spinal Muscular Atrophy.
abstract: Despite observed benefits of current treatments, several burdensome symptoms persist in people living with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). Fatigue is consistently indicated as a top unmet need by the SMA community. Historically ascribed as an inevitable consequence of underlying muscle weakness, fatigue is now recognized as central to the lived SMA experience, and several efforts have been made to better characterize it. As in other disorders, the study of fatigue in SMA is complicated by inconsistencies in terminology and nomenclature, a challenge compounded by the heterogeneous language patients use to describe their experiences. Without shared language and conceptual frameworks, progress toward an improved understanding of fatigue has been impeded. Critical to this aim is distinguishing between related but distinct constructs: perceived fatigue, a subjective multidimensional experience, and fatigability, a measurable decline in motor output or sustained activity. Both are prominent in SMA, but their biological causes remain unclear. Here, we draw on available evidence and the perspectives of experts, community stakeholders, caregivers, and patients to propose a uniform, collaboratively developed methodology that aims to advance SMA fatigue research and clinical management. This review outlines a roadmap to enhance identification of biological mechanisms and harmonize assessment tools, ultimately leading to a breakthrough in the treatment of fatigue. This iterative process is likely to extend beyond SMA and yield similar benefits in related neuromuscular conditions.

title: Sleep regularity associates with brain health in older adults.
journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
abstract: We examined the relationships between actigraphy-based regularity of sleep timing and brain aging outcomes among functionally unimpaired older adults. Participants included 149 older adults without dementia enrolled in studies at the University of California San Francisco. Participants completed neuropsychological testing and brain magnetic resonance imaging followed by 30 days of Fitbit Inspire 2 actigraphy monitoring to capture sleep regularity (i.e., day-to-day consistency in sleep/wake timing), average sleep duration, and variability in sleep duration. Linear regression examined cognitive and brain imaging outcomes as a function of sleep features, covarying for demographics. More consistent sleep regularity related to better global cognition, executive function, and memory; fewer depressive symptoms; larger brain volumes; fewer white matter hyperintensities; and better white matter integrity (Ps < 0.05). Sleep regularity was a stronger predictor than average sleep duration and variability in sleep duration for all outcomes. Consistency in sleep/wake timing (sleep regularity) is important for healthy brain aging.

title: Signs of Eagle Predation on a 22-kg Adult Primate.
abstract: Some researchers have adopted a 20 kg upper limit to avian predation on primates, with no confirmed cases exceeding 13 kg. Here, we report evidence of eagle interactions with adult male olive baboons (Papio anubis) and evaluate the implications for understanding past predation pressures during hominin evolution. Fieldwork was conducted in Réserve Naturelle et Culturelle d'Ennedi, Chad, in February-March 2025. Surveys of sandstone cliffs and talus deposits yielded cranial and postcranial remains of P. anubis, including proximal femora. We measured the superoinferior breadth of each femoral head to estimate body mass using established cercopithecid regression equations.
