Mice in the Age group had higher HM and EWAT (both P 0.05). PA was ∼50% lower in the Age group (8778 ± 5774 vs. 4132 ± 1523 rev/day), though Age-SA had 48% higher PA (Age-SA 6118 ± 2203 rev/day). SA treatment did not affect BM (37.8 ± 2.7 vs. 37.7 ± 3.2 g), EWAT (1.4 ± 0.4 vs. 1.3 ± 0.4 g) or HM (0.17 ± 0.01 vs. 0.19 ± 0.04 g, Age-Veh vs. Age-SA, all P > 0.05, respectively). GT AUC differed by group (P = 0.019), with Age-SA having lower AUC (Young 47120 ± 8751 vs. Age-SA 37180 ± 5383 AUC, P 0.22). SA reversed the age-associated reduction in complex I+II-driven respiration in adipose (P < 0.05). Ageing elevated adiposity, impaired pyruvate tolerance and reduced adipose mitochondrial function, though SA was partially restorative in mitigating these age-associated effects, warranting further study.

title: Age at Menarche, Temperament, and Eating Disorder Severity Across Diagnostic Subtypes: A Transdiagnostic Investigation in a Large Clinical Sample.
journal: The International journal of eating disorders
abstract: This study examined the timing of age at menarche relative to eating disorder (ED) onset across ED subtypes and tested whether temperamental traits moderated the link between pubertal timing and ED severity. The study comprised 3127 treatment-seeking women diagnosed with anorexia nervosa (AN), bulimia nervosa (BN), binge-eating disorder (BED), atypical AN, purging disorder (PD), and unspecified feeding or eating disorder (UFED). Age at current ED onset and age at menarche were assessed at intake using a semi-structured interview. ED symptom severity was measured using the Eating Disorder Inventory (EDI-2), and temperament and character were evaluated using the Temperament and Character Inventory-Revised (TCI-R). Participants, on average, reported ED onset at 19.7 years (SD = 7.85) and menarche at 12.47 years (SD = 1.61). ED diagnostic groups differed in both age at menarche and the interval between menarche and ED onset: BED was characterized by the earliest age of menarche and the longest gap of 12.4 years, whereas AN showed the latest age of menarche. Women whose age of menarche occurred after ED onset had significantly greater ED severity than those whose age of menarche preceded the ED onset. High harm avoidance and low self-directedness were consistently associated with greater ED severity, but temperament did not moderate the relationship between age of menarche and ED severity. Age of menarche is a clinically meaningful marker that varies across ED subtypes and is independently associated with ED severity, supporting its routine consideration in assessment and formulation.

title: Endothelial Cell-Pericyte Interplay in Ischemic Stroke: Unraveling Pathogenic Networks and Translational Frontiers.
abstract: Ischemic stroke remains a leading cause of death and long-term disability worldwide. Increasing evidence indicates that endothelial cell-pericyte (EC-PC) crosstalk is not merely a structural feature of the neurovascular unit, but a dynamic regulatory axis that shapes blood-brain barrier integrity, capillary tone, inflammatory trafficking, and vascular repair after ischemia. In this review, we synthesize current evidence into a stage-aware framework in which EC-PC communication shifts from homeostatic coupling to acute uncoupling, maladaptive remodeling, and, in favorable settings, reparative re-coupling. We summarize the principal molecular pathways governing this interaction, including PDGF, TGF-β, Notch, extracellular matrix signaling, exosomal communication, and adhesion-dependent mechanotransduction. We further discuss how disruption of this axis contributes to blood-brain barrier breakdown, inflammatory amplification, oxidative injury, aberrant angiogenesis, and impaired neurorestoration. Finally, we evaluate the translational implications of EC-PC crosstalk for biomarker discovery, imaging-based assessment, and targeted intervention, while highlighting key unresolved issues-particularly temporal heterogeneity, context-dependent signaling, and the gap between experimental models and human stroke-that must be addressed to move the field toward clinically actionable neurovascular therapies.

title: Late-onset Alzheimer's Disease Pathologies in a Novel hAβ/ApoE4 Mouse Line.
abstract: Most Alzheimer's disease (AD) cases are late-onset and sporadic, yet existing mouse models predominantly reflect familial, autosomal-dominant forms. To address this gap, we present the first characterisation of hAβ/ApoE4 mice, which carry a humanised amyloid-beta (Aβ) sequence knocked into the endogenous amyloid precursor protein (APP) locus and a human apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4) allele replacing murine ApoE, in the context of age-associated AD phenotypes. We aged hAβ/ApoE4 mice of both sexes to 12 months and assessed AD-relevant pathologies including cognition, spine loss, neurodegeneration, neuroinflammation and Aβ deposition. At 12 months, hAβ/ApoE4 mice exhibited spatial memory deficits in the Barnes maze as well as modestly reduced apical dendritic spine density without hippocampal neuronal loss. This model offers a platform for introducing environmental stressors and co-morbidities and establishes a reference point for the development of next-generation sporadic AD models.

title: Probiotics, Prebiotics, Synbiotics and the Gut-Brain Axis in Precision Health.
journal: Advances in experimental medicine and biology
abstract: The gastrointestinal system synthesizes a considerable proportion of the body's neurotransmitters and neuromodulators and is consequently increasingly acknowledged as the "second brain." Advances in high-throughput sequencing technology following the Human Genome Project have considerably expanded understanding of the gut microbiome, igniting increasing interest in microbiota-based medicinal approaches. Probiotics, defined as live microorganisms offering health benefits when provided in suitable doses, have proven potential in the management of chronic inflammatory and immune-mediated illnesses through immunomodulatory and barrier-protective pathways. The therapeutic efficacy of probiotics is strain-specific and influenced by dosage, host physiology, and environmental factors; consequently, strain selection prioritizes functional attributes such as gastrointestinal survivability, adhesion to intestinal epithelium, modulation of resident microbiota, and antimicrobial activity. Despite promising clinical and preclinical evidence, comprehensive elucidation of the systemic effects of probiotics and identification of novel symbiotic strains remain critical research priorities, underscoring the need for interdisciplinary collaboration between pharmacologists and microbiologists.Another highly integral aspect of nutrition and medical research involves prebiotics. Prebiotics are defined as selectively fermentable substances that promote the activity and number of beneficial microbes in the gastrointestinal region. Oligosaccharides and inulin are examples that add to the betterment of metabolic homeostasis and immune system functioning. The rising consumer education and innovation have led to large-scale expansion in the prebiotics industry, which strengthens the connection between microbiology, nutrition, and health economics.Synbiotics that combine both probiotics and prebiotics represent a cutting-edge strategy that can enhance the resistance and stability of gut microbiota, especially in the gut-brain axis (GBA) microbiota network. New multiomics approaches have revealed the intricate relationships that exist between the microbiota and the host that modulate neuropathological, metabolic, and immunological outcomes. There is a great variation in the microbial populations and corresponding metabolic products among different human subjects that clearly reveals the need to develop microbiota-targeting therapies.

title: Predicting others' actions through one's own motor style: Behavioral and neural evidence for a kinematic similarity effect.
abstract: Predictive processes during action observation are known to benefit from motor expertise, but it remains unclear which factors drive successful prediction in everyday actions, where everyone can be considered an "expert." We hypothesized that prediction accuracy is modulated not only by expertise per se, but by the degree of fine-grained kinematic overlap between the observer's and the agent's motor repertoire, here operationalized as motor similarity. In Study 1 (N = 90, action execution), we introduced a continuous, multidimensional, kinematics-based metric of inter-individual motor distance, and used it to quantify each participant's motor style relative to others. In Study 2 (N = 20, behavioral) and Study 3 (N = 21, behavioral and EEG), we then tailored action-observation tasks to each participant by selecting movements that varied parametrically in similarity to their own motor style, while verifying that stimuli across similarity levels carried equivalent amounts of action-relevant kinematic information. Behavioral results consistently showed that motor similarity enhances perceptual prediction: observers were more accurate when viewing actions that were closer to their individual motor style. Electrophysiological data further revealed that beta-band modulation, a neural signature associated with prediction uncertainty, is amplified over sensorimotor regions when participants observed more dissimilar movements. Together, these findings demonstrate that the degree of agent-observer kinematic overlap is a key determinant of prediction processes, extending beyond traditional expertise-based accounts.

title: Triggered electromyography-guided progressive fascicular subdivision to identify a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval in conjoined twin spinal cord separation: a dual-configuration case series.
journal: Child's nervous system : ChNS : official journal of the International Society for Pediatric Neurosurgery
abstract: Surgical separation of conjoined twins with fused caudal spinal cords requires identification of a safe neural cleavage plane, yet anatomical boundaries are often indistinct. Triggered electromyography (tEMG) has been used to determine nerve root ownership, and iterative subdivision with sequential stimulation has been reported in pygopagus twins, but the sequence and its endpoint have not been standardized. This study describes a tEMG-guided progressive fascicular subdivision approach to identify a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval in two conjoined twin configurations. We monitored two cases (pygopagus and ischiopagus) using multimodal intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, including tEMG, transcranial motor evoked potentials, somatosensory evoked potentials, and free-running electromyography. A dual-twin color-coded electrode configuration enabled simultaneous independent mapping of both nervous systems. Progressive fascicular subdivision with re-stimulation of each bundle was performed until a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval was identified. Case 1 involved pygopagus twins with a fused conus medullaris at S2. Case 2 involved ischiopagus twins with syringomyelia involving both spinal cords and an anterior sacral meningocele. In both cases, progressive fascicular subdivision identified a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval, which guided microsurgical separation. Motor function and anal tone were unchanged at 6-month follow-up. Triggered electromyography-guided progressive fascicular subdivision identified a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval in both pygopagus and ischiopagus configurations, including one with complex intrinsic spinal cord pathology. This interval reflects absence of detectable somatic motor activation in the monitored muscles and does not exclude sensory or autonomic fibers; its value as an intraoperative reference requires validation in larger series.
